decks.title: Human Health and Disease — Part 1: Infectious diseases
goals: Give the agent, transmission, symptoms and prevention of common viral and bacterial diseases
Explain the Widal test for typhoid
Describe amoebiasis, malaria with the life cycle of Plasmodium, ascariasis, filariasis and ringworm

slides.heading: Infectious diseases
slides.body_md: Part 1 — diseases caused by viruses, bacteria, protozoa, worms and fungi, and how to prevent them.

visual.alt: Flow from pathogen to transmission to symptoms to prevention

slides.narration: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens that pass from one person to another, directly or through air, water, food or vectors. For each disease we ask: what causes it, how it spreads, what it does, and how to prevent it.

slides.heading: Viral diseases
slides.body_md: Viruses multiply only inside host cells; antibiotics do not act on them.

rows: Infects nose and airways, not lungs: congestion, sore throat, cough, headache for 3–7 days
Chikungunya virus; bite of Aedes mosquito
Fever with severe, lasting joint pain, rash
High fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, joint and muscle pain, rash, fall in platelets

visual.alt: Table of viral diseases with agents, spread and symptoms

slides.narration: The common cold stays in the nose and throat. Chikungunya and dengue are spread by the same day-biting Aedes mosquito, which breeds in clean, stagnant water in coolers, tyres and pots. Dengue can lower the platelet count dangerously.

slides.heading: Bacterial diseases
slides.body_md: Many bacterial diseases can be treated with antibiotics and prevented by vaccines and hygiene.

rows: Salmonella typhi; contaminated food and water
Sustained high fever (39–40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache; intestinal perforation in severe cases
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae; droplets, shared glasses
Alveoli fill with fluid; fever, chills, cough; lips and nails may turn bluish
Sore throat, fever, a tough membrane in the throat; toxin may damage the heart
Yersinia pestis; bite of the rat flea
Fever, chills, swollen painful lymph nodes (buboes)

visual.alt: Table of bacterial diseases with agents, spread and symptoms

slides.narration: Typhoid spreads through food and water contaminated by faeces. Pneumonia and diphtheria spread through droplets in the air. Plague is carried by fleas from rats. Vaccines such as the D P T vaccine protect children against diphtheria.

slides.heading: Typhoid and the Widal test
slides.body_md: Typhoid is confirmed by the **Widal test**: the patient’s serum is diluted step by step and mixed with killed **Salmonella** antigens. If the serum has **antibodies**, the bacteria **clump (agglutinate)**. The **titre** is the highest dilution that still agglutinates.

rows: Agglutination at a high dilution (often 1 : 160 or more)
A healthy person who sheds the bacteria (for example, “Typhoid Mary”, a cook)

visual.alt: Table about typhoid and the Widal test

slides.narration: A high titre means the serum contains many antibodies against the typhoid bacterium, which is evidence of infection. Mary Mallon, a cook, was a healthy carrier who spread typhoid for years through the food she prepared.

slides.heading: Quick check: typhoid
slides.body_md: Which test confirms typhoid fever?
slides.narration: Quick check. The test is named after Fernand Widal.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a Widal test
slides.body_md: A patient’s serum was tested at dilutions of 1 : 20, 1 : 40, 1 : 80, 1 : 160, 1 : 320, 1 : 640. Agglutination was seen up to 1 : 160 and not beyond. What is the titre, and what does it suggest?
bullets: The **titre** is the highest dilution showing agglutination: **1 : 160**.
A titre this high suggests **active typhoid infection**, to be confirmed with symptoms and a blood culture.

visual.alt: Worked table: titre 1 : 160

slides.narration: Read down the table and stop at the last dilution that still clumps. The serum still had enough antibody at one in one hundred and sixty, which is high enough to suggest typhoid.

slides.heading: Amoebiasis
slides.body_md: **Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery)** is caused by the protozoan **Entamoeba histolytica**, a parasite of the **large intestine**.

rows: Food and water contaminated by faeces; houseflies act as mechanical carriers
Constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucus and blood clots
Clean drinking water, covered food, control of flies, proper disposal of faeces

visual.alt: Table about amoebiasis

slides.narration: Houseflies do not themselves get the disease; they carry cysts on their bodies from faeces to food. Clean water, covered food and sanitation break the chain.

slides.narration: Sporozoites injected by the mosquito multiply first in liver cells, then in red blood cells. When the red cells burst they release a toxin, haemozoin, which causes chill and high fever. Some parasites become gametocytes; a mosquito that bites the patient takes them up, and fertilisation happens in its gut.

slides.heading: The malaria fever cycle
slides.body_md: In **vivax malaria**, red blood cells burst together every **48 hours**, so bouts of **chill and high fever** recur at hours 0, 48, 96, 144 and so on.

visual.alt: Temperature chart of vivax malaria with fever bouts every 48 hours

slides.narration: Between bouts the temperature returns almost to normal. Each spike matches a fresh wave of red blood cells bursting and releasing haemozoin. That regular pattern helps doctors recognise malaria.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting the next bout
slides.body_md: A patient with vivax malaria had fever bouts at hours 0, 48, 96, 144 after the first one. When is the next bout expected, and why?
bullets: Interval $= 48 - 0 = 48$ hours.
Next bout $= 144 + 48 = 192$ hours.
Each bout marks the **synchronised bursting of red blood cells** at the end of each 48-hour cycle of multiplication.

visual.alt: Worked table: next bout at hour 192

slides.narration: The bouts are forty eight hours apart, so the next one should come forty eight hours after the last. Antimalarial drugs that stop the parasites multiplying in red cells break this cycle.

slides.heading: Worm and fungal diseases
slides.body_md: Parasitic worms (helminths) and fungi also cause common diseases.

rows: Roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides; eggs in soil, water and vegetables contaminated by faeces
Internal bleeding, muscle pain, fever, anaemia, blockage of the intestine
Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi; bite of female Culex mosquito
Chronic inflammation of lymph vessels of the legs: elephantiasis
Fungi Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton; contact, towels, combs, soil
Dry, scaly, itchy patches on skin, nails and scalp, especially in warm, moist folds

visual.alt: Table of worm and fungal diseases

slides.narration: Ascaris eggs pass out in faeces and are swallowed with dirty food or water. Filarial worms block lymph vessels so the legs swell enormously. Ringworm is not a worm at all, but a fungus that thrives in warm, moist skin.

slides.heading: Prevention and control
slides.body_md: Most infectious diseases can be prevented by breaking the chain of transmission.

rows: Clean body, safe water and food, washing hands
Proper disposal of waste and excreta, clean water supply
Draining stagnant water, mosquito nets, introducing Gambusia fish that eat larvae
Vaccines against typhoid, diphtheria, pneumonia and others

visual.alt: Table of prevention and control measures

slides.narration: Air-borne diseases need less crowding and covered coughs. Water-borne and food-borne diseases need clean water and sanitation. Vector-borne diseases need us to remove breeding places, for instance by draining standing water or releasing Gambusia fish.

slides.heading: Quick check: vectors
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about mosquitoes.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which mosquito spreads malaria, and which spreads dengue?

slides.heading: Quick check: haemozoin
slides.body_md: What causes the chill and high fever in malaria?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is released when red blood cells burst.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Viral: common cold (rhinoviruses), chikungunya and dengue (Aedes).
Bacterial: typhoid (Salmonella typhi, Widal test), pneumonia, diphtheria, plague (rat flea).
Protozoan: amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica, houseflies), malaria (Plasmodium, female Anopheles, haemozoin).
Helminths: ascariasis (Ascaris), filariasis (Wuchereria, Culex); fungal: ringworm.
Prevention: hygiene, vector control, vaccines, treatment.

visual.alt: Summary table of vectors and diseases

slides.narration: To recap: each disease has its own agent and route of spread. Knowing the route tells us how to break it, through hygiene, vector control, vaccines and treatment.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For each disease, give **agent, mode of spread, symptoms and prevention**.
Name the **vector** precisely: female Anopheles, Aedes, female Culex, rat flea.
Describe the **Plasmodium life cycle** in both hosts, with **haemozoin**.
Explain the **Widal test** with agglutination and titre.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give the agent, spread, symptoms and prevention for each disease. Name each vector exactly. Trace the malaria parasite through both hosts. And explain the Widal test in terms of clumping and titre.

decks.title: Human Health and Disease — Part 2: Cancer and allergies
goals: Distinguish benign and malignant tumours and describe the properties of cancer cells
List the causes of cancer and its methods of diagnosis and treatment
Define allergy and allergen, and state the general symptoms of allergy

slides.heading: Cancer and allergies
slides.body_md: Part 2 — when cell division escapes control, and when the immune system over-reacts.

visual.alt: Flow from normal cells to transformation to cancer cells to tumour and metastasis

slides.narration: In our bodies, cell growth and division are tightly controlled. Cancer begins when a cell escapes these controls and divides without limit. Allergy is a different problem: the immune system reacts too strongly to harmless substances.

slides.heading: Contact inhibition
slides.body_md: Normal cells show **contact inhibition**: when they touch their neighbours, they **stop dividing**. **Cancer cells** have **lost** this property, so they keep dividing and pile up into a mass of cells, a **tumour**.

slides.heading: Benign and malignant tumours
slides.body_md: **Benign tumours** stay confined to their original site, often inside a capsule, and do little damage. **Malignant tumours** are masses of **neoplastic** cells that grow rapidly, **invade** nearby tissue, starve normal cells, and spread through blood to distant sites — **metastasis**, the most feared property.

slides.narration: A benign tumour pushes on its surroundings but stays put. A malignant tumour sends cells into blood vessels, and they settle elsewhere to start new tumours. Metastasis is what makes cancer so dangerous.

slides.heading: Causes of cancer
slides.body_md: Agents that transform normal cells into cancer cells are **carcinogens**. They act by damaging DNA and activating **proto-oncogenes** (cellular oncogenes) into **oncogenes**.

rows: Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays); non-ionising ultraviolet light
Tobacco smoke (major cause of lung cancer), some industrial chemicals

visual.alt: Table of carcinogens by type

slides.narration: Ionising radiation and chemicals in tobacco smoke damage DNA directly. Some viruses carry their own cancer-causing genes. Normal cells also contain proto-oncogenes, which can turn into oncogenes when mutated.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how many divisions make a tumour?
slides.body_md: A tumour of about one billion cells (10⁹) is roughly one centimetre across. If it began from one cell that doubles at each division, how many rounds of division were needed?
bullets: After $k$ doublings there are $2^{k}$ cells.
So about **30** rounds of division were needed.

visual.alt: Worked table: about 30 doublings give 10 to the power 9 cells

slides.narration: Doubling is powerful. Ten doublings give about a thousand cells, twenty about a million, and thirty about a billion. A lump that can just be felt may already have gone through thirty rounds of uncontrolled division.

slides.heading: Diagnosis of cancer
slides.body_md: Early detection allows successful treatment of many cancers.

rows: A piece of suspected tissue is stained and examined under a microscope
X-rays, computed tomography (3-D X-ray images) and magnetic resonance imaging (strong magnetic fields) locate internal tumours
Genes that make a person likely to develop cancer

visual.alt: Table of methods of cancer diagnosis

slides.narration: A biopsy, looking at the tissue itself, is the surest test. Imaging methods find tumours deep inside the body without surgery, and molecular tests can identify people at higher risk before any tumour appears.

slides.heading: Treatment of cancer
slides.body_md: Treatment usually combines several methods.

rows: Kills tumour cells with lethal radiation, sparing surrounding tissue as far as possible
Drugs kill dividing cells; side effects include hair loss and anaemia
Biological response modifiers such as α-interferon activate the immune system against the tumour

visual.alt: Table of methods of cancer treatment

slides.narration: Chemotherapy drugs attack rapidly dividing cells, so they also affect hair follicles and bone marrow, which explains hair loss and anaemia. Tumour cells often avoid the immune system, so interferon is given to help the body destroy them.

slides.heading: Quick check: contact inhibition
slides.body_md: Which property do cancer cells lose?
slides.narration: Quick check. What stops normal cells dividing when they meet their neighbours?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: biopsy results
slides.body_md: A hospital laboratory examined 240 biopsies from lumps in one month; 36 showed malignant cells. What percentage were malignant, and what were the rest likely to be?
bullets: Malignant $= \dfrac{36}{240} \times 100 = 15$ percent.
The other **85 percent** were not cancerous — many lumps are **benign tumours** or other swellings.

visual.alt: Worked table: 15 percent malignant

slides.narration: Most lumps examined turned out not to be cancer, which is why a biopsy is needed before deciding on treatment. Histopathology tells benign from malignant tissue by the appearance of the cells.

slides.heading: Allergies
slides.body_md: An **allergy** is the **exaggerated response** of the immune system to certain harmless substances in the environment, called **allergens** — such as **dust mites, pollen and animal dander**. The body makes **IgE** antibodies; **mast cells** release **histamine and serotonin**.

nodes.label: Mast cells release histamine and serotonin

visual.alt: Flow of an allergic reaction from allergen to IgE to mast cells to symptoms

slides.narration: Symptoms include sneezing, watery eyes, a running nose and difficulty in breathing. Anti-histamines, adrenaline and steroids reduce them. Children in very clean modern homes may be more prone to allergies, perhaps because their immune systems meet fewer challenges early in life.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cancer cells lose contact inhibition and divide without control.
Benign tumours stay put; malignant tumours invade and metastasise.
Carcinogens: physical (radiation), chemical (tobacco), biological (oncogenic viruses); proto-oncogenes become oncogenes.
Diagnosis: biopsy and histopathology, blood tests, X-ray, CT, MRI, antibodies, molecular tests. Treatment: surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy (α-interferon).
Allergy: exaggerated response to allergens; IgE, histamine, serotonin; sneezing, watery eyes, breathing difficulty.

rows: Normal cells stop dividing on contact
Spread of cancer cells to new sites

visual.alt: Summary table of key terms

slides.narration: To recap: cancer is uncontrolled cell division, most dangerous when malignant cells metastasise. It has physical, chemical and biological causes, and is diagnosed and treated in several ways. Allergy is an over-reaction of the immune system to harmless allergens.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Contrast **benign** and **malignant** tumours in at least three points.
Name **contact inhibition** and **metastasis** as properties of cancer cells.
Give **one example** of each kind of carcinogen.
For allergy, name **IgE**, **mast cells** and **histamine**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Contrast benign and malignant tumours point by point. Use the terms contact inhibition and metastasis. Give an example of each kind of carcinogen. And for allergy, mention IgE, mast cells and histamine.

sections.heading: 1. Viral and bacterial diseases
sections.body_md:
**Health** is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. **Infectious diseases** are caused by **pathogens** and spread from person to person.

**Viral diseases**
- **Common cold** — **rhinoviruses**; infect the **nose and respiratory passages, not the lungs**. Nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache and tiredness lasting **3–7 days**. Spread by **droplets** from coughs and sneezes and by **contaminated objects** (pens, books, door handles).
- **Chikungunya** — chikungunya virus, spread by the bite of the **Aedes** mosquito; fever with **severe, prolonged joint pain**, rash.
- **Dengue** — dengue virus, spread by the **day-biting Aedes aegypti**; sudden high fever, severe headache, **pain behind the eyes**, joint and muscle pain (“break-bone fever”), rash, **fall in platelet count**; severe forms cause bleeding.

**Bacterial diseases**
- **Typhoid** — ***Salmonella typhi***; enters the **small intestine** with **contaminated food and water** and spreads to other organs. Sustained high fever (**39–40 °C**), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache, loss of appetite; **intestinal perforation** and death in severe cases. Confirmed by the **Widal test**. **Mary Mallon** (“Typhoid Mary”), a cook, was a **carrier** who spread typhoid for years.
- **Pneumonia** — ***Streptococcus pneumoniae*** and ***Haemophilus influenzae***; infects the **alveoli**, which fill with fluid, reducing respiration. Fever, chills, cough, headache; in severe cases **lips and fingernails turn grey to bluish**. Spread by **droplets** or by sharing glasses and utensils.
- **Diphtheria** — ***Corynebacterium diphtheriae***; sore throat, fever, a tough grey **membrane** in the throat that may block breathing; its **toxin** can damage the heart and nerves. Prevented by the **DPT vaccine**.
- **Plague** — ***Yersinia pestis***; spread by the bite of the **rat flea**; fever, chills, painful **swollen lymph nodes (buboes)** in bubonic plague; controlled by rodent control and antibiotics.

**Widal test.** The patient’s serum is serially diluted (1 : 20, 1 : 40, 1 : 80 …) and mixed with killed *Salmonella* antigens. **Agglutination** (clumping) shows antibodies against the bacterium. The **titre** is the highest dilution that still agglutinates; a high titre (for example 1 : 160) suggests active typhoid.

key_terms.definition_md: Agglutination test for antibodies against Salmonella typhi, confirming typhoid.
Infected person without symptoms who can spread a disease.
Highest dilution of serum that still gives a positive reaction.

sections.heading: 2. Protozoan, helminthic and fungal diseases; prevention
sections.body_md:
**Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery)** — the protozoan ***Entamoeba histolytica*** in the **large intestine**. Constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, **stools with excess mucus and blood clots**. **Houseflies** are **mechanical carriers** that transfer cysts from faeces to food and water.

**Malaria** — ***Plasmodium*** (*P. vivax*, *P. malariae*, *P. falciparum*; *P. falciparum* causes the most serious, malignant malaria). Vector: **female *Anopheles*** mosquito. **Life cycle (two hosts):**
1. An infected mosquito bites and injects **sporozoites** (infective stage).
2. Sporozoites multiply **asexually in liver cells**, then attack **red blood cells (RBCs)**, multiply there and burst them.
3. Bursting RBCs release the toxin **haemozoin**, which causes **chill and high fever**; in vivax malaria the bouts recur about every **48 hours** as RBCs burst together.
4. Some parasites develop into **gametocytes** in RBCs.
5. A female *Anopheles* takes up gametocytes with blood; **fertilisation** and development occur in the **mosquito’s stomach (gut) wall**.
6. **Sporozoites** formed there move to the mosquito’s **salivary glands**, ready to infect the next person.
The human is the **intermediate host** (asexual phase); the mosquito is the **definitive host** (sexual phase).

**Ascariasis** — the roundworm ***Ascaris lumbricoides*** in the intestine; internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, **anaemia** and **blockage of the intestine**. Eggs passed in faeces contaminate soil, water and vegetables.

**Filariasis (elephantiasis)** — ***Wuchereria bancrofti*** and ***W. malayi***; live in **lymphatic vessels**, mostly of the **lower limbs**, causing chronic inflammation and gross swelling; genital organs may be affected. Spread by the bite of the **female *Culex*** mosquito.

**Ringworm** — fungi of the genera ***Microsporum***, ***Trichophyton*** and ***Epidermophyton***; **dry, scaly lesions** on skin, nails and scalp with intense **itching**; favoured by **heat and moisture** (groin, between toes); spread through soil and shared towels, clothes and combs.

**Prevention and control:** **personal hygiene** (clean body, safe food and water); **public hygiene** (proper disposal of waste and excreta, clean water reservoirs); for air-borne diseases, avoid close contact with patients; for **vector-borne** diseases, remove stagnant water, use **mosquito nets** and screens, spray insecticides and introduce **Gambusia** fish that feed on mosquito larvae; **vaccination** and **antibiotics**.

Infective stage of Plasmodium injected by the mosquito.
Sexual stage of Plasmodium formed in RBCs and taken up by the mosquito.
Gross swelling of limbs due to filarial worms blocking lymph vessels.

sections.heading: 3. Cancer
sections.body_md:
**Cancer** is the uncontrolled division of cells. Normal cells show **contact inhibition**: contact with other cells stops their division. **Cancer cells lose contact inhibition**, divide continuously and form masses called **tumours**.

**Benign tumours** remain **confined** to their original location (often within a capsule), do not spread, and cause little damage. **Malignant tumours** are masses of proliferating **neoplastic** cells that grow rapidly, **invade** and damage surrounding tissue and compete with normal cells for nutrients. Cells sloughed from them reach distant sites through the **blood**, where they start new tumours: **metastasis**, the most feared property of malignant tumours. A tumour of about 10⁹ cells needs about **30** doublings from one cell.

**Causes (carcinogens):** **physical** — **ionising** radiation (X-rays, gamma rays) and **non-ionising** UV light damage DNA; **chemical** — **tobacco smoke** (the major cause of lung cancer) and some industrial chemicals; **biological** — **oncogenic viruses** carrying **viral oncogenes**. Normal cells carry **proto-oncogenes (cellular oncogenes, c-onc)**; when activated under certain conditions they cause oncogenic transformation.

**Diagnosis:** **biopsy and histopathology** of tissue; **blood and bone-marrow tests** (increased cell counts in leukaemia); **radiography (X-rays)**, **computed tomography (CT)** and **magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)**; **antibodies against cancer-specific antigens**; **molecular biology** techniques to detect genes that make a person susceptible.

**Treatment:** **surgery**; **radiation therapy** (lethal irradiation of tumour cells, protecting normal tissue); **chemotherapy** (drugs, many with side effects such as hair loss and anaemia); **immunotherapy** with **biological response modifiers** such as **α-interferon**, which activate the immune system, since tumour cells often avoid detection.

key_terms.definition_md: Stopping of cell division when cells touch their neighbours.
Spread of malignant tumour cells through blood to new sites.
Normal cellular gene that can become a cancer-causing oncogene.

sections.heading: 4. Allergies
sections.body_md:
An **allergy** is the **exaggerated response of the immune system** to certain antigens present in the environment. The substances that cause it are **allergens** — common ones are **mites in dust, pollen and animal dander (fur and skin flakes)**.

The antibodies produced are of the **IgE** type. On a later exposure, allergens bind IgE on **mast cells**, which release chemicals such as **histamine and serotonin**.

**General symptoms:** **sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing** (as in asthma); skin rashes may occur.

**Relief:** drugs such as **anti-histamines, adrenaline and steroids** quickly reduce the symptoms. Modern, very protected lifestyles may lower immunity and increase sensitivity to allergens.

key_terms.definition_md: Exaggerated immune response to a harmless environmental antigen.
Substance that causes an allergy, such as pollen or dust mites.
Chemical released by mast cells, causing allergic symptoms.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the common cold infects the lungs (it affects the nose and airways).
- Calling Aedes the malaria vector (malaria: female Anopheles; dengue and chikungunya: Aedes; filariasis: female Culex).
- Saying houseflies cause amoebiasis (they are mechanical carriers).
- Naming haemoglobin instead of haemozoin as the malaria toxin.
- Calling ringworm a worm infection (it is fungal).
- Saying benign tumours metastasise (only malignant ones do).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: an agent, a vector, a symptom, a test, a carcinogen.
- 2–3-mark questions: one disease in full; Widal test; benign vs malignant; causes or diagnosis of cancer; allergy.
- 5-mark questions in parts: life cycle of Plasmodium with diagram; comparison of diseases; cancer from cause to treatment.

questions.stem_md: Which laboratory test is used to confirm typhoid fever?
questions.solution_md: The Widal test detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi by agglutination — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student has nasal congestion, a sore throat and a hoarse voice for five days, but her chest examination and lungs are normal. Which is the most likely cause?
questions.solution_md: The common cold affects the nose and airways but not the lungs — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Several people in a colony have high fever, pain behind the eyes, joint pain and a falling platelet count. Mosquitoes that bite by day are breeding in water coolers. Which disease and vector are most likely?

options.text_md: Plague, spread by the rat flea

questions.solution_md: Day-biting Aedes in clean stored water; low platelets point to dengue — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a child with severe pneumonia, the lips and fingernails turn bluish grey. What is the reason?

options.text_md: The alveoli fill with fluid, so too little oxygen enters the blood.
The bacteria produce a blue pigment in the skin.
The heart stops pumping blood to the hands.
Red blood cells burst and release haemozoin.

questions.solution_md: Fluid-filled alveoli reduce gas exchange, causing cyanosis — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Plague caused by Yersinia pestis usually reaches humans through

options.text_md: the bite of the female Culex mosquito
the bite of the rat flea

questions.solution_md: Rat fleas carry Yersinia pestis from rodents to humans — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A tough grey membrane forming in the throat of a child with fever, which may block breathing, is typical of
questions.solution_md: Corynebacterium diphtheriae forms a membrane in the throat — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A healthy-looking cook can spread typhoid to many people.

**Reason (R):** Carriers can shed Salmonella typhi in their faeces without showing any symptoms.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the carrier state explains how a healthy cook spreads typhoid (as with Typhoid Mary) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A patient’s serum was tested in the Widal test at dilutions 1 : 10, 1 : 20, 1 : 40, 1 : 80, 1 : 160 and 1 : 320. Agglutination occurred in the first four tubes only. If the titre is written as 1 : n, what is n?
questions.solution_md: The highest dilution with agglutination is 1 : 80, so $n = 80$.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: antibiotics are of no use in treating the common cold.

answer.model_answer_md: The common cold is caused by **viruses (rhinoviruses)**; antibiotics act only on **bacteria**.

questions.solution_md: Viral disease.

marking_scheme.step: Viral cause; antibiotics act on bacteria

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: sharing drinking glasses with a pneumonia patient is risky.

answer.model_answer_md: Pneumonia bacteria spread through **droplets and aerosols** from an infected person, which can be left on **shared glasses and utensils**.

questions.solution_md: Droplet transmission.

questions.stem_md: The common cold is caused by a group of viruses called ______.
questions.solution_md: Rhinoviruses.

questions.stem_md: Dengue is spread by the day-biting mosquito Aedes ______.
questions.solution_md: Aedes aegypti.

questions.stem_md: Compare dengue and chikungunya with respect to their vector and one distinctive symptom of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Both are **viral** diseases spread by the bite of **Aedes** mosquitoes (dengue mainly by **Aedes aegypti**). **Dengue:** high fever with **pain behind the eyes** and a **fall in platelet count**. **Chikungunya:** fever with **severe, long-lasting joint pain**.

questions.solution_md: Same vector; different symptoms.

questions.stem_md: Name the causative organism and the mode of transmission of (i) pneumonia and (ii) plague.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Pneumonia** — ***Streptococcus pneumoniae*** (or *Haemophilus influenzae*); spread by **droplets/aerosols** from an infected person or by **sharing glasses and utensils**. (ii) **Plague** — ***Yersinia pestis***; spread by the **bite of the rat flea**.

questions.solution_md: Agents and transmission.

questions.stem_md: Describe typhoid fever with respect to its causative agent, mode of spread, symptoms and confirmatory test.

answer.model_answer_md: Typhoid is caused by the bacterium ***Salmonella typhi***, which enters the **small intestine** with **contaminated food and water** and spreads to other organs. Symptoms are **sustained high fever (39–40 °C)**, weakness, stomach pain, **constipation**, headache and loss of appetite; **intestinal perforation** and death may occur in severe cases. It is confirmed by the **Widal test**, which detects antibodies by agglutination.

questions.solution_md: Agent, spread, symptoms, test.

questions.stem_md: Explain the principle of the Widal test. Patient A’s serum agglutinates up to a dilution of 1 : 320; patient B’s serum does not agglutinate even at 1 : 20. Interpret both results.

answer.model_answer_md: The test is based on **antigen–antibody agglutination**: serum is **serially diluted** and mixed with killed ***Salmonella*** antigens; antibodies in the serum make the bacteria **clump**. The **titre** is the highest dilution that still agglutinates. **Patient A** has a **high titre (1 : 320)**, showing many antibodies — **likely typhoid**. **Patient B** has **no antibodies** against *Salmonella* — typhoid is **unlikely**.

questions.solution_md: Principle; interpretation.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the causative agent and two symptoms of typhoid, and name the test used to confirm it. [2]
(b) Explain how pneumonia affects the lungs and how it spreads. [2]
(c) A family boils its drinking water but keeps uncovered water in a cooler. Which of typhoid and dengue are they protected from? Explain. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) ***Salmonella typhi***; **sustained high fever (39–40 °C)**, **weakness, stomach pain and constipation**; confirmed by the **Widal test**.

(b) The bacteria (***Streptococcus pneumoniae***, *Haemophilus influenzae*) infect the **alveoli**, which **fill with fluid**, so less oxygen enters the blood; fever, chills and cough follow. It spreads by **droplets** and by **sharing glasses and utensils**.

(c) Boiling protects them from **typhoid** (water-borne), but the **open cooler** lets **Aedes** breed, so they are **not** protected from **dengue**.

questions.solution_md: Typhoid; pneumonia; prevention.

questions.stem_md: What causes the chill and high fever in a malaria patient?

options.text_md: Haemozoin released when infected red blood cells burst

questions.solution_md: Haemozoin is the toxin released from bursting RBCs — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which insect transmits malaria from one person to another?
questions.solution_md: Only female Anopheles transmit Plasmodium — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which stage of Plasmodium is injected into the human body when an infected mosquito bites?

options.text_md: Merozoite released from red blood cells

questions.solution_md: Sporozoites from the salivary glands are the infective stage — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Where do the gametes of Plasmodium fuse during its life cycle?

options.text_md: In the stomach (gut) of the female Anopheles
In the salivary glands of the mosquito

questions.solution_md: Fertilisation takes place in the mosquito’s stomach; the mosquito is the definitive host — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Removing stagnant water around homes helps to control both malaria and dengue.

**Reason (R):** The mosquitoes that spread these diseases lay their eggs and grow as larvae in water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and removing breeding water reduces both Anopheles and Aedes, which explains the assertion — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a village where flies swarm over uncovered food, many people pass stools containing mucus and blood clots. Which disease is likely, and what role do the flies play?

options.text_md: Typhoid; the flies are the definitive hosts
Amoebiasis; the flies act as mechanical carriers of cysts
Ascariasis; the flies lay worm eggs in the gut

questions.solution_md: Entamoeba histolytica cysts are carried from faeces to food by houseflies — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A man in a coastal district has grossly swollen legs after years of infection by worms that live in his lymph vessels. Which vector spread the infection?
questions.solution_md: Wuchereria is spread by female Culex; the swelling is elephantiasis — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A footballer who shares towels develops dry, scaly, very itchy patches between his toes. Which group of organisms is most likely responsible?
questions.solution_md: Ringworm is a fungal infection favoured by heat and moisture — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ascariasis can cause anaemia and blockage of the intestine.

**Reason (R):** Ascaris is a virus transmitted by the bite of mosquitoes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false: Ascaris is a roundworm whose eggs are swallowed with contaminated food or water — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A patient with vivax malaria has the first bout of fever at hour 0, and bouts recur every 48 hours. At which hour is the fifth bout expected?
questions.solution_md: Fifth bout $= 0 + 4 \times 48 = 192$ hours.

questions.stem_md: The species of Plasmodium that causes the most serious, malignant malaria is Plasmodium ______.
questions.solution_md: Plasmodium falciparum.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Gambusia fish are released into ponds in areas where malaria is common.

answer.model_answer_md: Gambusia **feed on mosquito larvae**, reducing the number of **Anopheles** that can spread malaria.

questions.solution_md: Eat larvae.

questions.stem_md: Describe the part of the life cycle of Plasmodium that takes place inside the female Anopheles mosquito.

answer.model_answer_md: The mosquito takes up **gametocytes** with the blood of an infected person. In its **stomach**, gametes form and **fertilise**, and the zygote develops in the **stomach wall**. **Sporozoites** are produced, which move to the **salivary glands** and are injected at the **next bite**.

questions.solution_md: Gametocytes to sporozoites.

marking_scheme.step: Gametocytes taken up; fertilisation in stomach

questions.stem_md: Name the causative agent and give one symptom of (i) ascariasis and (ii) filariasis.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Ascariasis** — the roundworm ***Ascaris lumbricoides***; causes **internal bleeding, anaemia** or **blockage of the intestine**. (ii) **Filariasis** — ***Wuchereria bancrofti*** (or *W. malayi*); causes chronic inflammation of lymph vessels and gross **swelling of the legs (elephantiasis)**.

questions.solution_md: Agents and symptoms.

questions.stem_md: Describe the development of Plasmodium inside the human body after an infected mosquito bite.

answer.model_answer_md: The mosquito injects **sporozoites**, which reach the **liver** and multiply **asexually** in liver cells. Their products then invade **red blood cells**, multiply and **burst** them, releasing **haemozoin**, which causes **chill and high fever**; in vivax malaria this recurs about every **48 hours**. Some parasites in the red cells develop into **gametocytes**, which are taken up by a mosquito when it bites.

questions.solution_md: Liver, RBCs, gametocytes.

questions.stem_md: A town reports outbreaks of malaria, amoebiasis and ringworm. Suggest one specific preventive measure for each disease, explaining how it breaks transmission.

answer.model_answer_md: **Malaria:** drain stagnant water, use **mosquito nets** or release **Gambusia** — fewer **Anopheles** mosquitoes bite people. **Amoebiasis:** **cover food**, control **houseflies** and ensure **sanitation and clean water** — cysts no longer reach food and drink. **Ringworm:** keep skin **dry** and do **not share towels, combs or clothes** — fungal spores are not passed on.

questions.solution_md: One measure each.

questions.stem_md: Compare malaria and filariasis with respect to the causative agent, the vector and the part of the body chiefly affected.

answer.model_answer_md: **Agent:** malaria — the protozoan ***Plasmodium***; filariasis — the roundworms ***Wuchereria bancrofti*** and *W. malayi*. **Vector:** malaria — **female *Anopheles***; filariasis — **female *Culex***. **Part affected:** malaria — **liver cells and red blood cells**, causing recurring fever; filariasis — **lymphatic vessels**, mostly of the legs, causing **elephantiasis**.

questions.solution_md: Three comparisons.

questions.stem_md:
(a) With the help of a labelled flow diagram, describe the life cycle of Plasmodium in its two hosts. [3]
(b) Why does fever in vivax malaria recur at regular intervals? [1]
(c) Why do only female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Human (asexual phase):** **sporozoites** injected by the mosquito → multiply in **liver cells** → invade **RBCs**, multiply and **burst** them, releasing **haemozoin** → some form **gametocytes**. **Mosquito (sexual phase):** female *Anopheles* takes up **gametocytes** → **fertilisation** in the **stomach** → development in the stomach wall → **sporozoites** move to the **salivary glands** → injected at the next bite.

(b) Parasites in RBCs complete their multiplication **together**, so RBCs **burst at the same time** about every **48 hours**, releasing haemozoin each time.

(c) Only **females suck blood** (for egg development), so only they take up and inject the parasite.

questions.stem_md: Describe three methods used to detect cancer, stating what each reveals.

questions.stem_md: After surgery to remove a tumour, a few cancer cells may remain in a patient. Explain how radiation therapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy could each help, mentioning one drawback or special feature of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Radiation therapy** irradiates the remaining tumour cells lethally; care is needed to **protect surrounding normal tissue**. **Chemotherapy** uses drugs that kill **dividing cells**; it has side effects such as **hair loss and anaemia**. **Immunotherapy** uses **biological response modifiers** such as **α-interferon** to **activate the patient’s immune system**, which tumour cells otherwise often escape.

questions.stem_md: In a laboratory, cells from tissue X form a single layer in a dish and then stop dividing. Cells from tissue Y keep dividing and pile up in layers, and when injected into a mouse they produce tumours in its lungs and liver. Interpret these observations.

answer.model_answer_md: Tissue **X** cells show **contact inhibition**: on touching neighbours they stop dividing — they are **normal**. Tissue **Y** cells have **lost contact inhibition**, so they divide **without control** and form a mass — they are **cancer (transformed) cells**. Tumours appearing in **distant organs** show that Y cells can enter the blood and **metastasise**, so Y is **malignant**.

questions.solution_md: Normal vs malignant.

questions.stem_md:

(b) Describe the three types of carcinogens with one example each. [2]
(c) Why does giving up smoking reduce a person’s risk of lung cancer? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Contact inhibition** is the property of normal cells by which **contact with other cells stops their division**; cancer cells lose it and pile up into tumours. **Metastasis** is the spread of **cells from a malignant tumour** through the **blood** to distant sites, where they form **new tumours**.

(b) **Physical:** **ionising radiation** (X-rays, gamma rays) and **UV light** damage DNA. **Chemical:** **tobacco smoke** and some industrial chemicals. **Biological:** **oncogenic viruses** with viral oncogenes.

(c) Tobacco smoke contains **chemical carcinogens** that **damage DNA** in lung cells and can activate **proto-oncogenes**; stopping smoking **removes this exposure**.

questions.stem_md: A boy sneezes and wheezes every spring but is free of symptoms in winter. Explain, step by step, what happens in his body from first contact with the allergen to the appearance of symptoms.

answer.model_answer_md: In spring the air carries **pollen**, an **allergen**. At **first exposure**, his immune system makes **IgE antibodies** against it, which attach to **mast cells**. On **later exposure**, pollen binds these IgE molecules, and the mast cells **release histamine and serotonin**, which cause **sneezing, watery eyes, a running nose and narrowing of airways (wheezing)**. In winter there is **little pollen**, so no reaction occurs.

(c) Name two kinds of drugs used to relieve allergy symptoms. [1]
(d) Suggest why children brought up in very protected, over-clean surroundings may be more prone to allergies. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An **exaggerated immune response** to harmless environmental antigens; **pollen, dust mites, animal dander**.

(b) The body makes **IgE antibodies** against the allergen; they **bind to mast cells**. On re-exposure the allergen links these IgE molecules and the **mast cells release histamine** (and serotonin), which **dilates blood vessels and narrows airways**, causing sneezing, watery eyes and breathing difficulty.

(c) **Anti-histamines**, **adrenaline** and **steroids**.

(d) Their immune systems meet **fewer microbes and antigens early in life**, so **immunity is lowered** and they become **more sensitive** to harmless allergens.
